acceptable.choice: Stay on Java 21 + Spring Boot (3.2+) and turn on virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true), keeping blocking-style code
acceptable.why: The roughly 200-request ceiling is Tomcat's default worker pool of 200 threads, not a limit of Java; virtual threads let one thread per waiting request scale to 10,000 cheaply, using the approved stack and the team's existing skills.

acceptable.choice: Spring MVC async request handling (DeferredResult / CompletableFuture / Callable) on Tomcat
acceptable.why: It frees the servlet worker thread while the request waits for the payment confirmation, uses only standard Spring features, and works on Boot versions that predate virtual-thread support.

acceptable.choice: Spring WebFlux on Reactor Netty (reactive, non-blocking)
acceptable.why: It is part of the Spring portfolio and handles tens of thousands of idle connections well, but the reactive style is harder to write, debug and audit than virtual threads, so it is a valid second choice rather than the default.

acceptable.choice: Event-driven correlation: hold requests in an in-memory map keyed by correlation ID, completed by Kafka confirmation events (or a callback)
acceptable.why: This is the right architecture for the wait itself: no thread spins or polls per request, and it fits the Kafka already in their stack.

acceptable.choice: Asynchronous API contract (202 Accepted plus a callback/webhook, or polling) as a longer-term option, if partner banks agree
acceptable.why: It removes long-held connections altogether, but it changes the partner contract, so it is a negotiation and not a quick fix.

ruled_out.why: Go is not on the approved-technology list, adding it means a months-long security review, and Java can already handle this load.
Not on the approved list (months-long language security review), the team doesn't have the skills, and it brings supply-chain and long-term-support concerns for a bank.
Same approved-list and security-review problem, the team lacks the skills, and the problem doesn't require them.
Kotlin is a separate language that may need its own approval, and Java 21 virtual threads already give the same benefit.

ruled_out.choice: Switch to Quarkus, Micronaut, Vert.x or raw Netty
ruled_out.why: These are new frameworks outside the Spring standard, likely off the approved list, and they add governance and support burden without being needed.

ruled_out.choice: Just raise server.tomcat.threads.max to about 10,000 platform threads
ruled_out.why: It is a memory-heavy, fragile workaround (stack per thread, context switching) when virtual threads or async servlets fix the root cause properly.

ruled_out.choice: Scale out to dozens of pods to multiply the 200-thread limit
ruled_out.why: It wastes on-prem OpenShift capacity and hides a configuration and threading-model problem instead of fixing it.

must_mention: No new language or framework is needed: the roughly 200 ceiling matches Tomcat's default max worker threads (server.tomcat.threads.max=200), so this is thread-per-request exhaustion, not a Java or Spring limitation.
The recommended fix is Java 21 virtual threads in Spring Boot 3.2+ (or async servlet / DeferredResult), which keeps the team on the approved stack with no security review.

Raise the other connection limits too: Tomcat server.tomcat.max-connections (default 8192 with NIO, below 10,000 per instance if one pod takes all the load), accept-count, OS file-descriptor limits (ulimit), and container memory per pod.

Check timeouts along the whole path: the OpenShift router/HAProxy default route timeout is 30s, which exactly matches the 30s wait and must be raised (haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout). The same goes for any F5 or external load-balancer idle timeouts and the server's async request timeout.
Do not hold a JDBC connection, or any pooled resource, while waiting: with 10,000 waiters a Hikari/Oracle pool will run out long before threads do.

Virtual-thread pinning on Java 21: synchronized blocks and some drivers (for example older Oracle JDBC, other libraries) can pin carrier threads. Use current driver versions, check with JFR (jdk.VirtualThreadPinned), and note that JEP 491 (fixed in JDK 24+) is not in 21 LTS.

Correlating responses across replicas: a Kafka confirmation may be consumed by a different pod or data centre than the one holding the connection, so the design needs routing (e.g. per-instance reply topics, or broadcast with a local lookup) and a plan for what happens when a pod restarts.
Little's law sanity check: a few hundred completions per second × up to 30s ≈ thousands to 10,000 concurrent waiters. That load is moderate for the JVM, and the work is I/O-bound waiting, not CPU.
Prove it with a load test (e.g. Gatling or JMeter, both Java-based) at 10,000 concurrent long-held connections across both data centres before production.
red_flags: Recommending a language change (Go, Node.js, Rust, Elixir) as needed or as the main answer, ignoring the approved list and the months-long security review.
Claiming Java or Spring Boot inherently can't handle 10,000 concurrent connections.

Recommending a move to WebFlux/reactive as mandatory without mentioning virtual threads, or without noting the cost of reactive complexity for a 600-engineer organisation that cares about maintainability.
Proposing non-approved frameworks or libraries (Vert.x, Quarkus, Akka/Pekko, Kotlin) without flagging that they need architecture-board approval.
Fixing only the thread count while ignoring max-connections, router/load-balancer timeouts, file descriptors, and DB connection pool exhaustion, so the system just fails at the next limit.
Suggesting polling loops or Thread.sleep inside request threads to wait for confirmations.
Ignoring cross-pod and cross-data-centre correlation of Kafka confirmations, which breaks once there is more than one replica.
Recommending non-LTS JDKs (e.g. JDK 24/25 just for the pinning fix) without addressing long-term support policy, or recommending Spring Boot versions out of support.
Recommending managed cloud services (AWS API Gateway, Lambda, etc.) when the platform is on-prem OpenShift.
unknowns: The exact Spring Boot version and servlet container (virtual-thread support needs Boot 3.2+), and whether the prototype uses Spring MVC or WebFlux.
What the request thread does while waiting (blocking on a JDBC query, polling a table, a blocking Kafka consume, a synchronized wait), which determines both the fix and the pinning risk.
Which JDBC driver, HTTP client and other libraries are in use, and whether they pin virtual threads on Java 21.
The network path and its limits: OpenShift router configuration, F5/external load balancers, mTLS termination for partner banks, and their idle and connection limits.
How payment confirmations arrive (Kafka topic, callback, core-banking system) and how they can be routed to the pod holding the request across two data centres.
Whether partner banks could accept an async contract (callback/webhook or polling) instead of holding connections open.
Whether virtual threads and WebFlux count as already approved under the Java/Spring entry or need any architecture-board sign-off.
Required behaviour on timeout and on pod failover (retry semantics, idempotency, audit trail of in-flight requests).
Actual throughput and latency once fixed, which must be measured by load testing at the target concurrency.
